children: By Paul Vieira and Amanda Coletta

Canada and the European Union will begin talks next month on a new security and economic alliance, the latest bold step by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney to reduce his country's economic reliance on the U.S.

Carney delivered the news Tuesday at an investment summit he's hosting in Toronto, where some of the world's biggest investors - from Wall Street heavyweights like Blackstone and BlackRock to sovereign-wealth funds from Norway and Abu Dhabi - are attending as the Canadian leader makes a pitch for their investment dollars.
Late Tuesday, Carney is traveling to Europe where he's set to deliver remarks to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France. In remarks at the summit, Carney provided a preview of what's ahead.
"Next month, we will begin discussions with the EU - the world's second-largest economy - to build a unique security and economic alliance," Carney said.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Saturday that Carney instructed his special envoy to Europe to scope out the most ambitious possibilities short of full membership in the EU or its common market, according to people familiar with the matter. Canadian and European officials are discussing ways for Canada to informally lock into Europe's $20 trillion single market in key supply chains, the Journal reported.

A senior Canadian official said this week's trip - which also includes a stop in Liverpool for a meeting with U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham - is meant to lay the groundwork for a EU-Canada summit in Montreal next month.

At a press conference, Carney said Canada is realigning its economic and diplomatic strategy amid an upheaval globally, stemming from a protectionist trade policy from the Trump administration to China's dominance over manufacturing and critical minerals. Policy decisions in Washington are having the biggest impact, as Canada has historically counted on trade with the U.S. as a significant driver of economic growth.

When it comes to the EU, "there's areas where we come together and fit together," said Carney, who studied in England and previously served as the Bank of England governor. He cited as examples conventional and clean energy, critical minerals, artificial intelligence and space technology. "The real deepening and discussions will be launched with our summit in Montreal."

The move to seek a special alliance with the EU comes amid a sharp deterioration in trade ties between Ottawa and Washington. The two capitals are mired in a heightened trade conflict after talks on a deal to provide tariff relief collapsed last month. Both countries have now imposed hefty tariffs on each other's exports, with Trump threatening a potentially crippling 50% tariff on Canadian-made motor vehicles and auto parts as early as Jan. 1.
Carney said that Canada would continue to be the U.S.'s most important partner in many key areas.

"These arrangements work when we engage as true partners that respect each other's traditions and sovereignty," he said. "When those opportunities return, Canada will be an even better partner-stronger, more resilient, more independent-ready to advance our mutual economic and security interests."

In a fireside-chat format after his speech, Carney said the global economy is in "a time when integration and sovereignty are in friction. For countries that want to retain sovereignty - and Canada wants to retain sovereignty for all the right reasons, including our unique culture - we need to use our assets to an advantage and pair with those that complement them."
